chapter_title: Python on Raspberry Pi: Setup, Tools, and First Program
chapter_summary:
Python is the most popular programming language for the Raspberry Pi. It is pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS, it has a clean and readable syntax, and it has powerful libraries for GPIO control, data analysis, web development, and machine learning. The Raspberry Pi Foundation officially recommends Python for physical computing, and the `gpiozero` library is written specifically for Python.

Raspberry Pi OS includes at least two versions of Python. `python3` is the current version, Python 3, and is the one you should use. `python` without the `3` may still point to Python 2 on some older systems, but Python 2 is no longer supported. When you write Python code, always call it with `python3`.

You can run Python interactively by opening a terminal and typing:

```bash
python3
```

This opens the Python REPL, which stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop. It lets you type Python commands one at a time and see immediate results. It is excellent for quick experiments. To exit, type `exit()` or press Ctrl+D.

You can also write Python code in a file and run it. Create a file called `hello.py`:

```python
print("Hello, Raspberry Pi!")
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Nice to meet you, {name}!")
```

Run it with:

```bash
python3 hello.py
```

The Raspberry Pi OS desktop includes **Thonny**, a beginner-friendly Python IDE. Thonny highlights syntax, helps you debug, and can run programs with a single click. It is a good choice when you are learning because it shows variables, errors, and the call stack in a simple interface. You can also use VS Code, which can be installed through `apt` or downloaded from Microsoft.

A Python program is just a text file with a `.py` extension. The file can contain functions, classes, variables, and statements. When you run the file, the Python interpreter reads it from top to bottom and executes each line. Unlike compiled languages such as C, Python code is interpreted at runtime, which makes development faster but execution slower.

Python uses indentation to define blocks of code. For example, the body of a function or a loop must be indented consistently, usually by four spaces. This is different from languages that use braces. Proper indentation is not optional in Python; it is part of the syntax.

narration.text: Welcome. In this module you'll learn why Python is the recommended language for Raspberry Pi projects, how to use the built-in tools to write and run programs, and how to create a simple interactive script. Python ships with Raspberry Pi OS and is chosen because it combines readable syntax with libraries that directly support hardware control. You will see two main ways to run Python: the interactive REPL for quick experiments and saved scripts for repeatable programs. We'll demonstrate writing a short program that prints a greeting and asks for a name, then run it both inside the Thonny editor and from the terminal using the Python three command. Along the way you'll learn to identify the correct interpreter version, avoid common indentation mistakes, and use simple input and output functions safely. By the end you'll be able to write a small script, run it from the desktop and the command line, and understand why the interpreter reads files line by line. Consider why the REPL is useful for experimenting and why scripts are essential for reproducible projects.

screens.title: Why Python is the Raspberry Pi language
screens.subtitle: Readability, libraries, and Foundation recommendation

narration.text: Python is the most common language used on Raspberry Pi because it balances readability, breadth of libraries, and direct access to hardware support. Readable syntax makes it easier to learn and maintain projects that interact with sensors, LEDs, and motors. For hardware control there are Python libraries specifically written for the Pi, such as gpiozero, which wraps lower-level interfaces and provides a simple A P I. The Raspberry Pi Foundation recommends Python for physical computing; that recommendation helps beginners by pointing them to a mature ecosystem. A concrete example: to blink an LED you can import a gpiozero class and call simple methods rather than manage low-level timing and registers. A common misconception is that Python is too slow for hardware work. While Python is interpreted and slower than compiled languages for tight loops, almost all Raspberry Pi hobby projects use Python for control logic and delegate time-critical tasks to libraries or hardware. In practice the speed tradeoff allows much faster development and clearer code. Remember: choose Python for speed of development and library access; consider lower-level languages only for specialized performance constraints. How might readability help when you return to a project after weeks away?

keyIdea.title: Readable and practical
keyIdea.text: Python's readable syntax and dedicated libraries like gpiozero make hardware projects faster to build and easier to maintain.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Why Python
Definition

Python combines simple, readable syntax with libraries written for the Raspberry Pi, enabling quick prototyping and clear code for hardware interaction.

Analogy

Think of Python as a high-level toolkit: it saves time the way a screwdriver speeds fastening compared to shaping nails by hand.

Practical example: gpiozero exposes simple LED controls; you call methods rather than manage hardware registers.
Misconception: Python is 'too slow'—for most Pi projects control code is fine; optimize only when performance issues arise.
Why it matters
  • Faster development with clear code reduces bugs in hardware projects.
  • A mature library ecosystem provides sensor drivers and helpers.
  • The Foundation's recommendation creates a large community and tutorials.
Key Takeaway

Python prioritizes developer speed and library support, which is ideal for Raspberry Pi learning and projects.

screens.title: Python versions on Raspberry Pi
screens.subtitle: Why you must call python3 and avoid Python 2 confusion

narration.text: Raspberry Pi OS may provide multiple Python executables. The safe rule is to use Python three because Python three is the supported, modern version. Historically systems provided a bare python name that pointed to Python 2, which is now end-of-life and unsupported. Calling python without the three can accidentally run an older interpreter on some systems. A useful approach is to explicitly type Python three when running the REPL or scripts. Concretely, when you type Python three in a terminal you enter an interactive session that uses the current Python three interpreter. When you run Python three script dot P Y file the interpreter executes the file. A common misconception is that both commands always behave the same on every system. They do not: some environments alias python to Python three, others do not. Check your system by running Python three --version and python --version to see which interpreter responds. If python shows version two, always prefer Python three. This habit prevents runtime errors caused by language differences, like print being a statement in older versions versus a function in Python three. Ask yourself: how could mismatched versions affect third-party libraries?

keyIdea.title: Use python3 consistently
keyIdea.text: Always invoke python3 explicitly to ensure you're using the supported interpreter and avoid legacy behavior from Python 2.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Python Versions
Quick checks
$ python3 --version
Python 3.x.x

$ python --version
Python 2.7.x  # possible on older systems
If python reports a 2.x version, always use python3 to run scripts and avoid syntax mismatches.
Contrast
Python 2 (legacy)

Older syntax and no longer supported; some keywords behave differently.

Python 3 (current)

Modern features, widely supported libraries, and the version to use on Raspberry Pi.

Common Mistake

Typing python instead of python3 can silently run the wrong interpreter and produce confusing errors.

screens.title: How the Python interpreter runs a script
screens.subtitle: What happens when you run python3 script.py

narration.text: When you run a Python script using Python three followed by a file name the interpreter performs a predictable sequence of steps. First it opens and reads the file content into memory, parsing the source into internal structures. Then it executes statements from top to bottom, creating variables, calling functions, and importing modules as needed. Any runtime errors such as syntax or indentation mistakes are reported with a file name and a line number so you can trace the problem. This interpreted workflow contrasts with compiled languages where source is transformed to machine code ahead of time. A concrete example: running hello dot P Y file that calls the print function and then input will execute the print statement first, then pause waiting for user input, then continue to the next print. A common misconception is that the interpreter executes lines out of order; it does not—control flow constructs like functions, loops, and conditionals control execution order. Understanding this top-to-bottom model helps you place initialization code at the top and interactive prompts at the point you want user interaction. Ask: where would you place setup code for hardware initialization in a script?

keyIdea.title: Top-to-bottom execution
keyIdea.text: Python reads a .py file, parses it, and executes statements in order unless control structures change the flow.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Interpreter Flow
Execution steps
  1. Open and read the file into memory.
  2. Parse source into structures and check syntax.
  3. Execute statements from top to bottom.
  4. Report errors with tracebacks and line numbers.
This process means order matters: put setup code before actions that depend on it.
Concrete example
# hello.py
print("Hello, Raspberry Pi!")
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Nice to meet you, {name}!")
Running python3 hello.py prints the greeting, waits for your input, then prints the response. Errors point to specific lines to help debugging.
Key Takeaway

Scripts execute sequentially; place code in the order you want it to run and use control structures to change flow.

narration.text: The REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop. It is an interactive session you start by typing Python three with no file argument. The REPL reads the expression you type, evaluates it immediately, prints the result, and then waits for your next input. This makes it ideal for small experiments: try arithmetic, inspect types, import a module and call a function to see immediate output. For example you can type a print call or simple arithmetic and see results at once, which helps to test ideas before writing a script file. A practical use is testing a library call to ensure it behaves as expected, then copying the working code into a script. A common misconception is that REPL sessions are saved automatically; they are not. If you want repeatability, put code into a dot P Y file file and run it as a script. Also respect that the REPL's environment is transient—variables live only in that session until you save them to a file. Reflect: what small expression would you test first in the REPL when starting a new project? REPL: Read‑Eval‑Print Loop means use the repl for immediate feedback and prototyping, then move tested code into scripts for repeatable runs.. In practical terms, interactive experimentation with immediate feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quick experiments
keyIdea.text: Use the REPL for immediate feedback and prototyping, then move tested code into scripts for repeatable runs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › REPL
What the REPL does
  • Read the expression you type.
  • Evaluate it immediately.
  • Print the result and wait for more input.
Good for testing functions, library calls, and trying expressions before making a script.
REPL example
$ python3
>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> print('Hi')
Hi
>>> exit()
Remember that the session is temporary. Copy working lines into a file to save them.
Pro Tip

Use the REPL to confirm small pieces of logic before placing them in a script file for repeatable runs.

screens.title: Write and run hello.py
screens.subtitle: A simple interactive script using print and input

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal but practical program you will write first. The file, named hello dot P Y file, uses the print function to show a greeting, then calls input to ask the user's name, and finally prints a personalized message. When run with Python three hello dot P Y file the interpreter executes statements in order: print runs, input pauses for the user to type, and the next print shows the collected name. This pattern introduces basic program flow and console interaction. In Thonny you can paste the same code and press run; Thonny will show the program output and may display variables in a side panel. A common error is forgetting to save the file before running it from the terminal, which will run the previous version instead. Always save changes. Another frequent issue is mismatched quotes or missing parentheses; the interpreter will report a syntax error with a line number. Practice saving, running, and intentionally causing and fixing a simple error to make debugging familiar. What would you change to ask the user for their favorite number instead?

keyIdea.title: First script flow
keyIdea.text: hello.py demonstrates printing, pausing for user input, and continuing execution when input is received.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › hello.py Walkthrough
Code example
print("Hello, Raspberry Pi!")
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Nice to meet you, {name}!")
Save this as hello.py and run python3 hello.py to try it. Thonny provides a one-click run alternative and a variables view.
Explanation
  • The print function outputs text to the console.
  • The input function waits for user input and returns it as a string.
  • Formatted printing inserts the captured name into the final message.
Key Takeaway

This simple program teaches input/output, sequence, and saving files for repeatable execution.

screens.title: Thonny: a beginner-friendly IDE
screens.subtitle: How Thonny supports learning and debugging

narration.text: Thonny is the default beginner IDE included with Raspberry Pi OS and it is built to reduce friction for learners. It highlights syntax, shows errors clearly, and provides a simplified debugger and variables view. This reduces the cognitive load when you're starting: you can see values change as your program runs and step through code without configuring complex settings. Thonny's single-click run is useful for writing and testing small scripts like hello dot P Y file. For learners who later prefer more advanced features, V S Code is an alternative that can be installed. A practical approach is to start in Thonny to learn syntax and program flow, then gradually move to a more advanced editor when you need features like extensions, integrated terminals, or version control. A common misconception is that an IDE automatically fixes logic errors; it helps you inspect state and find mistakes faster but you still must reason about program behavior. Try writing hello dot P Y file in Thonny, run it, then open the variables viewer to observe the name variable after supplying input. Thonny: a beginner-friendly IDE means use thonny to visualize variables and errors while learning; migrate to more feature-rich editors later as needed.. In practical terms, how thonny supports learning and debugging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Thonny eases debugging

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Thonny IDE
What Thonny provides
  • Syntax highlighting and simple run controls.
  • Variable viewer to inspect program state.
  • Beginner-friendly debugger and clear error messages.

Common Mistake

Assuming the IDE will correct logic errors. It helps you inspect state, but reasoning and fixes are manual.

screens.title: Running scripts in the terminal
screens.subtitle: Save, open terminal, and run with python3

narration.text: Running scripts from the terminal is a core skill for Raspberry Pi projects. The process is straightforward: create or save a dot P Y file file, open a terminal, navigate to the folder containing the file, and run Python three file_name dot P Y file. The terminal run is repeatable and helpful when you automate tasks or run scripts on boot. A concrete example: save add dot P Y file, open a terminal, use cd to reach the directory, and type Python three add dot P Y file to run. If the file isn't saved your last edits won't be included. Errors and tracebacks appear in the terminal with the file name and line number, which helps you quickly locate issues. A common mistake is running the wrong interpreter; always use Python three to ensure correct behavior. Another practical tip: if your script requires hardware access or permissions, run from an account with appropriate privileges or configure the necessary access. Consider: how would you run a script at startup later in a project? Running scripts in the terminal means use python3 file.py after saving your code; the terminal is ideal for automation and repeatable execution.. In practical terms, save, open terminal, and run with python3. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Terminal runs are repeatable
keyIdea.text: Use python3 file.py after saving your code; the terminal is ideal for automation and repeatable execution.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Terminal Run
Steps
$ cd /path/to/project
$ python3 add.py
Ensure the file is saved before running. The terminal shows tracebacks and error lines for debugging.
When to use the terminal
  • Running scripts repeatedly or on schedule.
  • Deploying code to run at boot or via automation.
  • Testing behavior outside an IDE environment.
Pro Tip

Use the terminal for automation and when a script must run without a graphical session.

screens.title: Indentation is syntax
screens.subtitle: Spaces define blocks; consistency prevents errors

narration.text: Indentation in Python is not optional decoration — it is part of the language syntax. Blocks such as function bodies, loops, and conditional branches are defined by consistent indentation, usually four spaces per level. Mixing tabs and spaces or using inconsistent indentation levels will produce an IndentationError or other syntax errors. This is different from languages that use braces or keywords to mark blocks. A practical example: a for loop requires the loop body to be indented; forgetting to indent the following line will raise an error. When learning, configure your editor to insert spaces instead of tabs and to display invisible characters if you encounter strange errors. A common misunderstanding is that any amount of indentation is acceptable; what matters is consistent alignment. If you see an unexpected IndentationError, check for mixing tabs and spaces and for accidental extra indentation. Reflect: how can editor settings reduce these indentation issues when you switch between machines? Indentation is syntax means always use consistent spaces for block structure; configure your editor to avoid mixing tabs and spaces.. In practical terms, spaces define blocks; consistency prevents errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Indentation matters
keyIdea.text: Always use consistent spaces for block structure; configure your editor to avoid mixing tabs and spaces.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Indentation
Rules
  • Indentation defines block scope in Python.
  • Use consistent spaces (commonly four) and avoid mixing tabs.
  • Errors refer to the line number to help find mismatches.
Example error
for i in range(3):
print(i)  # IndentationError: expected an indented block
Fix by indenting the print line with consistent spaces. Configure your editor to convert tabs to spaces to avoid this issue.

screens.title: Create add.py: add two numbers
screens.subtitle: Practice I/O, conversion, and running from terminal

narration.text: This hands-on activity reinforces input and output along with simple data conversion. Create a file named add dot P Y file that asks the user for two numbers, converts the inputs to numeric types, adds them, and prints the result. A simple pattern uses input to collect strings, then int or float to convert before adding. For example, input returns text; adding without conversion concatenates strings rather than performing numeric addition. A common mistake is forgetting to convert, which yields unexpected results. First run it in Thonny, enter test numbers like 2 and 3 to confirm the printed 5 result, then save and run it in the terminal with Python three add dot P Y file. This sequence helps you understand the REPL and script workflows, and shows why explicit conversion matters in user interactions. Consider edge cases such as non-numeric input and how you might handle them in later lessons with try-except blocks. What validation would you add to ensure robust input? Create add.py: add two numbers means use int() or float() to convert input strings to numbers; otherwise you risk string concatenation instead of numeric addition.. In practical terms, practice i/o, conversion, and running from terminal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Convert inputs before adding
keyIdea.text: Use int() or float() to convert input strings to numbers; otherwise you risk string concatenation instead of numeric addition.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › add.py Activity
Starter code
# add.py
x = input("Enter first number: ")
y = input("Enter second number: ")
# Convert to numbers before adding
sum = float(x) + float(y)
print(f"The sum is {sum}")
Run in Thonny first, then save and run with python3 add.py in a terminal to test repeatable behavior.
Common pitfalls
  • Not converting input causes string concatenation.
  • Not handling invalid input can crash the script.
Try this

Add validation with try-except to prompt again if the user types non-numeric input.

screens.title: Interpreted vs compiled languages
screens.subtitle: Why Python's interpreted nature matters for learning

narration.text: Python is an interpreted language, which means the interpreter reads and executes code at runtime rather than compiling it to machine code ahead of time. For learners this produces a faster feedback loop: you can edit a script and re-run it immediately without a separate compile step. This accelerates experimentation and debugging. However, being interpreted can make some programs slower than equivalent compiled programs written in languages like C. In Raspberry Pi projects this is usually acceptable because control logic and glue code benefit more from fast iteration, while performance-critical routines can live in optimized libraries. A concrete contrast: changing a print statement and re-running a Python script takes seconds in the interpreter workflow; in a compiled language you'd need to recompile before running. A common misconception is that interpreted equals low quality—it's a tradeoff: development speed and library support versus raw execution speed. Think about which parts of a system need speed and which need clear, maintainable code. Interpreted vs compiled languages means interpreted code enables rapid experimentation and easier learning; optimize later only where performance requires it.. In practical terms, why python's interpreted nature matters for learning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tradeoff: speed vs development time
keyIdea.text: Interpreted code enables rapid experimentation and easier learning; optimize later only where performance requires it.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Interpreted vs Compiled
Interpreted (Python)
  • Fast edit-test cycles and interactive REPL.
  • No separate compilation step.
  • Good for prototyping and hardware control logic.
Compiled (e.g., C)
  • Requires a compilation step before running.
  • Typically faster at runtime for compute-heavy tasks.
  • Useful when performance is critical.
Practical advice

Use Python for control and rapid development. If a part becomes a bottleneck, replace or extend it with optimized libraries or compiled modules while keeping the rest in Python.

narration.text: When you start writing Python on Raspberry Pi you'll encounter a few recurring errors. SyntaxError occurs when the interpreter cannot parse your code, often due to missing parentheses, unmatched quotes, or incorrect punctuation. IndentationError happens when block indentation is inconsistent. NameError indicates a variable name wasn't defined before use. Using the wrong interpreter produces different exceptions or unexpected behavior if Python 2 runs instead of Python three. The fastest fixes are: read the traceback carefully to find the file and line number, inspect the surrounding lines for mismatched punctuation or indentation, and verify you're running Python three. If an input-based script doesn't behave as expected, confirm the inputs are converted to the expected types. For persistent issues, use Thonny's error highlighting or run the script in the terminal to see the raw traceback. Practicing deliberately causing and fixing small errors accelerates your debugging skills and makes future issues less intimidating. Common errors and quick fixes means tracebacks point to the file and line number; use them with editor tools to locate and fix syntax or indentation issues quickly.. In practical terms, syntax, indentation, and wrong interpreter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Read tracebacks
keyIdea.text: Tracebacks point to the file and line number; use them with editor tools to locate and fix syntax or indentation issues quickly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Troubleshooting
Common errors
  • SyntaxError — check parentheses and quotes.
  • IndentationError — ensure consistent spaces, not tabs.
  • NameError — define variables before use.
Quick fixes
  1. Read the traceback to find the line number.
  2. Open the file in Thonny to see highlighted errors.
  3. Confirm you run python3 and save files before execution.
Remember

Errors are learning signals. Tracebacks guide you to the problem line — use them to iteratively fix and re-run your code.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts to keep in mind. First, always use Python three on Raspberry Pi to run the supported interpreter. Second, the REPL is a quick way to test ideas interactively, while dot P Y file script files are for repeatable execution. Third, Thonny is the recommended beginner IDE because it highlights syntax and shows variables, making debugging easier. Fourth, Python uses indentation for block structure; consistent spaces are essential. Fifth, print and input provide simple console interaction and require conversion of input when numeric operations are needed. These points form a practical toolkit: use the REPL to prototype, save working code to scripts, run scripts in Thonny or the terminal, and rely on explicit conversions and correct indentation to avoid common errors.
